conditions.title: Content
conditions.text: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } Protest and democracy From mass demonstrations to occupations and acts of civil disobedience: political dissent is not an unfamiliar phenomenon in democratic societies. Generally, (the possibility of) political dissent is often thought to be a ‘litmus test’ for democracy, but at the same time, its specific role and scope remain a continuous topic of debate. After all, even though political dissent and protest are, in a certain way, viewed as an important part of democratic politics, democratic regimes also already consist of (electoral) procedures and institutions that are generally considered to be ‘democratic’. In this thesis group, we will therefore reflect on the challenges and questions facing democratic theory when considering the role, value, and significance of protest within democratic regimes and societies. What have been influential forms of protest, and what was their democratic significance? Which principles—or which conception—of democracy is at stake when we regard certain forms of protest as democratic or undemocratic? How can we make sense of the role of political dissent and protest in the context of contemporary democratic politics?

conditions.title: Content
conditions.text: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } Group 1: Objectivity – Marij van Strien Is there such a thing as objective fact? Is it possible to be objective, or are we always caught in a particular subjective perspective? And what exactly does objectivity mean: detached, value-free, disinterested, neutral, factual, true? In this group, we will reflect on these questions, from the perspectives of the history of philosophy and the philosophy of science. From a historical perspective, we can recognize that the concept of objectivity itself has a history: what is seen as objective or subjective has shifted over time. Philosophers of science have traditionally argued that objectivity is essential in science, in the sense that values should play no role in science, so that scientific results can be accepted by anyone independently of their personal values. However, this ideal of value-free science has been increasingly criticized in the last few decades. In what ways do values play a role in science, and is it possible to retain some sense of objectivity in science despite this? Group 2: The rationality of conspiracy theories and theorists – Harmen Ghijsen Conspiracy theories and conspiracy theorists are often viewed as completely irrational. But is this frame the right one? Some philosophers have argued that, depending on the definition of "conspiracy theory", conspiracy theories need not be any less rational than other types of theories. Others have gone as far as to claim that not believing in conspiracy theories would be utterly naive. Starting from this perspective, you will investigate the philosophical literature on conspiracy theories and come up with your own research question related to the rationality of conspiracy theories and theorists. Group 3: Attraction & Disgust – Rae Aumiller Why do I suddenly experience ick toward a new crush? Why am I weirdly attracted to things that are kind of nasty? How do enemies suddenly become lovers? Is it possible for friend groups or political groups to be bound by what they hate as much as what they love? What is the relationship between fetish and phobia? Why do some racists sexualize those whom they discriminate? Why are some closeted queers the biggest homophobes? Hobbes claims that attraction and disgust spring from the same sense of bodily arousal. If this is true, what causes an individual, in the last instance, to lunge toward the object that arouses them or shrink away in disgust? The relationship between attraction and repulsion can be explored through phenomenology, existentialism, psychoanalysis, feminism, queer theory, and political philosophy (for starters). It lends itself to an analysis of sex and desire, sensation and emotions, sociality and politics, ethics, and aesthetic genres like horror and camp. Group 4: Power and Resistance in Digital Times– Guilel Treiber Even if we do not assume that the Internet and digitalization are qualitatively different from other political dynamics, and even if we accept that they are merely different mediums through which we are doing what politics has always been about, it is hard to contest that they have introduced in the last decade or so dramatic changes in the way we govern ourselves and others. In other terms, the distinction between an analog, brick-and-mortar political world oriented towards streets, squares, and parliaments and a digital, online world used as a tool to facilitate access, accountability, and supervision of government has collapsed. For example, there is no longer any logic in speaking of online or offline protest, given that most protest is both. This Bachelor Thesis Course aims to allow students to develop their understanding of the political and ethical implications of digitalization. It develops on themes addressed in the Digital Revolution module and encourages questions about what kind of power and possible resistance digitalization (broadly construed) allows for. Group 5: ​​​ Ethics and Aesthetics – Sophie Höfer This thesis group focusses on the relationship between ethics and aesthetics. As the realm of sensory experience and pleasure, an aesthetic lifestyle has often been contrasted with an ethical and responsible way of life, with thinkers like Leo Tolstoy going as far as to suggest that specific forms of art, especially music, are used by the devil to seduce human beings to immoral behaviour. Other thinkers have argued for a reconcilability of aesthetics and ethics: For the Romantics, an aesthetic appreciation of nature can equal a religious-ethical experience. From the 18th and 19th century to the current day, the relation between ethics and aesthetics raises questions like: How can an aesthetically enjoyable and an ethically responsible life be reconciled? Is an aesthetic life necessarily interesting and an ethical life necessarily boring? What (if any) is the ethical value of aesthetic experience? And is there aesthetic value in moral virtues? Can the cultivation of aesthetic appreciation in ourselves make us morally better or worse persons? What makes an aesthetic genius, and can there be something like an ethical genius? In this thesis group, you will develop your own research project exploring the relationship between ethics and aesthetics. Group 6: NNB – NNB ...
